splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps Auer/Kisor deference to agency interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions when lenity would favor the defendant. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity trumps deference. This affects how criminal defendants are sentenced under ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary takes precedence over the rule of lenity when construing ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when construing ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, such that Application Note 1 (which includes them) is not entitled to deference under Kisor/Stinson.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses, is a valid interpretation entitled to deference. Some circuits defer to the commentary, while others hold the guideline text is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) is ambiguous as to inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy is a reasonable interpretation entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) is clear on its face and does not include inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) or if possessing any one is disqualifying. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits read 'and' conjunctively, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits read it disjunctively. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenders.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its plain conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. The Eighth Circuit holds that state-law offenses qualify regardless of federal scheduling, while other circuits have required the substance to be federally controlled. This affects base offense levels and career-offender designations.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the career offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense,' so state convictions qualify even if the substance is not federally scheduled.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under federal law, applying a categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement at U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) validly authorizes such reductions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive statutory changes can support compassionate release motions. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits have permitted courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this but the Seventh Circuit held it exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission lacks authority to override Congress's decision not to make changes retroactive.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as part of the totality of circumstances when evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons exist for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions regarding conditions or terms of confinement (such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must be brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging not just the fact or duration of confinement but also the conditions and terms of confinement. The Eighth Circuit has acknowledged this unresolved conflict spanning more than half a century, affecting claims including First Step Act earned-time-credit disputes. The split determines which procedural vehicle — habeas or civil action — governs prisoner challenges to BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim seeks a speedier release or transfer to prerelease custody, habeas corpus under § 2241 is the sole federal remedy, consistent with Preiser v. Rodriguez.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may be available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP program decisions that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of confinement may be brought via civil rights actions rather than habeas.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the original Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor. This affects whether a Chapter 7 trustee can sell appreciated assets to satisfy creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad scope of § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and the purpose of § 348(f) protect good-faith converting debtors by keeping post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation out of the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation hearings, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the need for deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that supervised release revocation cannot be based on retributive punishment. The Sixth Circuit's dissenters note this places their court at the extreme of a circuit split, affecting hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider punishment as a purpose when imposing sentences upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that the statutory purposes of revocation sentences under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e) do not include punishment, and revocation should focus on deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter (subject to a 60-day appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fees motion is ancillary to the criminal case, but acknowledged a circuit split on this issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because a Hyde Amendment motion arises from and is inextricably linked to a criminal prosecution, it remains a criminal matter subject to the shorter criminal appeal deadline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA must be locked in by the end of the prior plan year (the statutory measurement date) or whether the actuary may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the statutory framework requires all actuarial assumptions to be determined by the end of the prior plan year, providing employers with greater predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary retains discretion to select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond what was specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke beyond the originally imposed term.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for judicially created fugitive tolling of supervised release, and the term expires as specified in the judgment regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars relitigating any previously presented claim — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter bar than the requirements in § 2255(h) alone.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the gatekeeping bar of § 2244(b)(1), which prevents relitigating previously raised claims, applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners bringing successive § 2255 motions need only satisfy the requirements of § 2255(h) and are not subject to the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category of orders as immediately appealable, creating potential divergence in the application of the collateral order doctrine to privacy-related sealing motions.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is a collateral order immediately appealable under § 1291 because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal does not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment or through other means.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures and ballot-counting rules. Some circuits grant candidates broad standing based on competitive injury, while others require more particularized harm. The resolution affects whether voting rule challenges can proceed before elections or must wait until post-election disputes arise.

positions.label: Candidates have standing for pre-election challenges
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law allegedly changes the rules governing ballot counting in ways that could affect election outcomes.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing for pre-election challenges
positions.summary: Holds that candidates cannot demonstrate a sufficiently concrete and particularized injury from ballot-counting rules to establish Article III standing before an election takes place.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination liability and damages in hospitality and business establishments was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide by establishing or refining standards for fair treatment and available remedies.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied a particular framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that other circuits may not follow.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims and available remedies in public accommodation and hospitality contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
